newsitem.title: USA: EEOC, Texaco close to settlement.
newsitem.headline: EEOC, Texaco close to settlement.

text.p: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is close to reaching an agreement with Texaco Inc. ahead of a hearing Friday over plans to assure the company's compliance with anti-discrimination law, an EEOC lawyer said Thursday.

The plans are related to a tentative settlement reached in November between Texaco and lawyers representing black employees who sued the oil company alleging they were discriminated against in pay and promotions.

A hearing on the settlement and the EEOC's proposal is scheduled before U.S. District Judge Charles Brieant in White Plains federal court at 11:30 a.m. EST on Friday. Lawyers said they planned to present a status report on the settlement talks and the judge was not expected to rule on the proposal.
In November, Texaco tentatively agreed to settle the discrimination suit by paying $176.1 million and establishing an "equality and tolerance" task force.
However, the EEOC was disturbed that it had been excluded from the settlement talks and petitioned the court to intervene in the case.

A final settlement of the discrimination suit has been delayed while Texaco and the EEOC have held negotiations on any possible monitoring role the federal agency might take, lawyers involved in the case said.

"We're very close," said EEOC lawyer Elizabeth Grossman. She would not comment on details of the plan except to say it focuses on future compliance with laws that prohibit discrimination in the workplace.

As part of Texaco's settlement with black employees, the company released a plan last month to boost employment, career development and recruiting of minorities as well as increasing purchasing from minority- and women-owned companies.

The plan was well-received by lawyers representing the black plaintiffs and the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who responded by calling for an end to the consumer boycott of Texaco he helped initiate in November.

Problems at Texaco surfaced after plaintiffs' lawyers in the discrimination suit received secret tapes of senior executives discussing the destruction of damaging documents. The executives allegedly also made racist remarks.
